title: Die Haselruthe
source: Brüder Grimm, Kinder- und Hausmärchen, Band 2, 7. Auflage (Ausgabe letzter Hand), Dieterich, Göttingen 1857, KHM 210. Text from Wikisource („Die Haselruthe (1857)“, twice proofread against the original). Fresh translation made directly from the German; 1857 spelling preserved exactly.
about: The last of the ten Kinderlegenden that close the Grimms' collection: on an afternoon when the Christ Child lies asleep in his cradle, his mother goes into the wood to gather strawberries for when he wakes, and a snake springs up out of the grass at her feet. She flees and hides behind a hazel bush until it has crawled away, and going home declares that as the hazel sheltered her, it shall protect others too — which is why, the tale says, a green hazel branch has ever since been the surest defence against adders and snakes.

sentences.t: Eines Nachmittags hatte sich das Christkind in sein Wiegenbett gelegt und war eingeschlafen,
sentences.l: One afternoon the Christ child had laid himself down in his cradle-bed and had fallen asleep,
sentences.i: One afternoon the Christ child had laid himself down in his cradle and had fallen asleep,
sentences.n: “Eines Nachmittags” is the genitive-of-time — “on an afternoon, one afternoon.” “Christkind” (Christ + Kind) is the Christ child, the infant Jesus. “Wiegenbett” = Wiege (cradle) + Bett (bed) — a cradle, a rocking-bed. “sich gelegt” is reflexive (legen + sich, to lay oneself down).

sentences.t: da trat seine Mutter heran, sah es voll Freude an und sprach „hast du dich schlafen gelegt, mein Kind? schlaf sanft, ich will derweil in den Wald gehen und eine Handvoll Erdbeeren für dich holen; ich weiß wohl, du freust dich darüber, wenn du aufgewacht bist.“
sentences.l: then his mother stepped up, looked at him full of joy and spoke, “have you laid yourself down to sleep, my child? Sleep soft, I will meanwhile go into the wood and fetch a handful of strawberries for you; I know well, you will be glad of it when you have woken.”
sentences.i: then his mother came up, looked at him full of joy and said, “have you laid yourself down to sleep, my child? Sleep sweetly; meanwhile I will go into the wood and fetch a handful of strawberries for you — I know you will be glad of them when you have woken.”
sentences.n: “trat … heran” is separable herantreten — to step up to (someone). “sah … an” is separable ansehen — to look at. “derweil” = meanwhile, in the meantime (old adverb). “sich freuen über” + accusative = to be glad of, to rejoice at. Read “du/dich/dir” throughout as English “you/you/you.”

sentences.t: Draußen im Wald fand sie einen Platz mit den schönsten Erdbeeren,
sentences.l: Out in the wood she found a place with the finest strawberries,
sentences.i: Out in the wood she found a patch of the finest strawberries,
sentences.n: “den schönsten Erdbeeren” — dative plural, superlative of schön with the strong -sten ending. “Erdbeeren” (Erde + Beeren) = earth-berries, strawberries.

sentences.t: als sie sich aber herabbückt um eine zu brechen, so springt aus dem Gras eine Natter in die Höhe.
sentences.l: but as she stoops down to pluck one, an adder springs up out of the grass.
sentences.i: but as she bends down to pluck one, an adder springs up out of the grass.
sentences.n: The narrative shifts into the present tense here (bückt, springt, erschrickt, schießt, versteckt, spricht) — Grimm often does this for the suddenness of a moment. “sich herabbücken” is reflexive and separable (herab-, downwards toward the speaker) — to bend down. “Natter” is an adder, a snake — usually a smooth non-venomous kind in German usage, but read here as a threatening snake.

sentences.t: Sie erschrickt, läßt die Beere stehen und eilt hinweg.
sentences.l: She takes fright, lets the berry stand and hastens away.
sentences.i: She takes fright, leaves the berry lying and hastens away.
sentences.n: “erschrickt” is the strong verb erschrecken in its intransitive sense — to be startled, to take fright (erschrickt/erschrak/erschrocken). “läßt … stehen” = to leave [something] standing, i.e. leave it where it is (läßt is the 1857 spelling of lässt). “hinweg” = away, off (hin + weg).

sentences.t: Die Natter schießt ihr nach, aber die Mutter Gottes, das könnt ihr denken, weiß guten Rath,
sentences.l: The adder shoots after her, but the Mother of God, that you can imagine, knows good counsel,
sentences.i: The adder darts after her, but the Mother of God, as you can imagine, knows a good remedy,
sentences.n: “schießt ihr nach” — separable nachschießen with a dative of the pursued: shoots after her. “das könnt ihr denken” is an aside to the reader — the narrator’s wink; “ihr” is second-person plural “you.” “Rath” is the 1857 spelling of Rat — counsel, advice, and by extension a good plan or remedy.

sentences.t: sie versteckt sich hinter eine Haselstaude und bleibt da stehen, bis die Natter sich wieder verkrochen hat.
sentences.l: she hides herself behind a hazel bush and remains standing there, until the adder has crept away again.
sentences.i: she hides behind a hazel bush and stays standing there until the adder has crept away again.
sentences.n: “Haselstaude” = Hasel (hazel) + Staude (a bushy shrub) — a hazel bush. “bleibt … stehen” = remains standing (bleiben + bare infinitive). “verkrochen” is the past participle of verkriechen — to creep away, crawl into hiding.

sentences.t: Sie sammelt dann die Beeren, und als sie sich auf den Heimweg macht, spricht sie „wie die Haselstaude diesmal mein Schutz gewesen ist, so soll sie es auch in Zukunft andern Menschen sein.“
sentences.l: She then gathers the berries, and as she makes her way home, she speaks, “as the hazel bush has been my shelter this time, so shall she also be it in future to other people.”
sentences.i: She then gathers the berries, and as she sets out for home, she says, “as the hazel bush has been my shelter this time, so shall it be so, in future too, for other people.”
sentences.n: “sich auf den Heimweg machen” = to set out on the way home, to head for home. “die Haselstaude … sie” — Staude is feminine, and the pronouns “sie … sie … sie” all point back to her; English carries the plant as “it.” The saying gives the aetiology: this is why the hazel is a protection.

sentences.t: Darum ist seit den ältesten Zeiten ein grüner Haselzweig gegen Nattern, Schlangen und was sonst auf der Erde kriecht, der sicherste Schutz.
sentences.l: Therefore since the oldest times a green hazel twig is against adders, snakes and whatever else creeps on the earth, the safest protection.
sentences.i: Therefore, since the oldest times, a green hazel branch has been the surest protection against adders, snakes, and whatever else creeps upon the earth.
sentences.n: “Darum” = for that reason, therefore — the tale’s closing formula. “Haselzweig” = Hasel (hazel) + Zweig (twig, branch) — a hazel switch, the same shrub as the Haselstaude and the title’s Haselruthe. The switch here is a Marian protective charm, not an instrument of punishment; the tale’s use is aetiological.

glossary.grüner: grün — green (masc. nom. sg. strong ending after ein; “ein grüner Haselzweig”)
glossary.sammelt: sammeln — gathers (3rd sg. present; “sie sammelt … die Beeren”)
glossary.versteckt: verstecken — hides (3rd sg. present; reflexive, sich verstecken)
glossary.weiß: wissen — know (1st sg. present; “ich weiß wohl” = I know well)
